Source: Asher & Lascarides (2008), Commitments, Beliefs and Intentions in Dialogue [1]
Retrieval Status: Substantive full text retrieved; the audit covered the dialogue-content and cognitive-logic sections. [1]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: Each participant has an SDRS representing the content to which that participant is currently publicly committed; grounding at a turn is content entailed by each SDRS. Public commitment is indexed by an agent and a group. [1]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: Utterances make public-commitment announcements that update the cognitive-logic model; the framework also supplies defeasible links from commitments to belief and intention. [1]
Operational Consequence: The stated consequence is a changed dialogue/cognitive state—grounded content, belief, intention, and predicted next dialogue moves—not a role- or artifact-governed workplace transition. [1]
Repair Contestability: Correction relations appear in worked dialogue analysis, but the retrieved text does not specify a participant-facing challenge or audit interface. [1]
Initial Audit Verdict: Very strong predecessor for actor-indexed public commitment and formal update; the unlocated link is authority- and artifact-governed operational promotion with human contestation. [1]

Source: Venant & Asher (2015), Dynamics of Public Commitments in Dialogue [2]
Retrieval Status: Substantive full text retrieved, including formal semantics, acknowledgement/correction analysis, and conclusions. [2]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: A dialogue act publicly commits an agent to possibly ambiguous content; the framework explicitly represents nested commitments and defines common commitment for a group. [2]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: Conversational moves are interpreted as action structures that update the model. A confirming question followed by a consonant answer licenses a move to common commitment. [2]
Operational Consequence: The transition changes the commitment slate and common-commitment status. The paper treats this as a dialogue-semantic consequence, not as an organizational permission, artifact, responsibility, or workflow-state update. [2]
Repair Contestability: Acknowledgements can ground commitments, while corrections and self-corrections remove prior commitments; correction can destabilize common-commitment goals. [2]
Initial Audit Verdict: The strongest direct threat to a claim about ambiguity-conditioned public-commitment promotion and revision. PCC’s remaining distinction must rest on operational governance and inspectable contestation, not on commitment dynamics alone. [2]

Source: Khebour et al. (2024), Common Ground Tracking in Multimodal Dialogue [3]
Retrieval Status: Substantive full text retrieved, including its shared-state data structure, evidence logic, closure rules, and evaluation. [3]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: The Common Ground Structure comprises a QBank of open task questions, an EBank of propositions with evidence, and an FBank of propositions believed true by all participants. [3]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: A public announcement moves a proposition from QBank to EBank; a repeated announcement such as ACCEPT promotes it from EBank to FBank. STATEMENT moves add evidence for or against candidate values. [3]
Operational Consequence: The implemented consequence is an update of the shared common-ground banks. The paper does not, in the retrieved text, specify role-based authorization, persistent organizational artifacts, or a participant-facing challenge process. [3]
Repair Contestability: The method includes evidence for and against alternatives and a DOUBT-related cognitive state, but no explicit retraction, appeal, or contestability protocol was located in the retrieved text. [3]
Initial Audit Verdict: Closest computational comparator for evidence-to-shared-state promotion. The critical residual test is whether PCC adds a genuinely distinct governance layer rather than a relabeling of QBank–EBank–FBank closure. [3]

Source: Tsvilodub et al. (2026), Act or Clarify? [4]
Retrieval Status: Substantive preprint full text retrieved, including two experiments, the expected-regret model, and limitations. [4]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: The formal model represents an individual decision problem: contextual goals, a probability distribution over those goals, available actions, and a utility function. It does not define a persistent actor-indexed common-ground state. [4]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: When expected regret is high, the agent may seek clarification to update the decision problem; otherwise it selects an action through a soft-max policy over expected utility. [4]
Operational Consequence: The choice is between a clarification question and direct linguistic or non-linguistic action. In the experiments, clarification became more likely with uncertainty or higher error cost. [4]
Repair Contestability: Clarification is modeled as information seeking. The retrieved model does not specify public evidence, role authority, a shared action-state transition, or an inspectable appeal mechanism. [4]
Initial Audit Verdict: Strong baseline for action-sensitive clarification, but not a near-equivalent to a multi-actor public-warrant architecture. Its key contribution to inherit is the uncertainty–cost decision rule. [4]

Source: Piwek (1997), Situated Action and Commitment in Dialogue [5]
Retrieval Status: Only the abstract-level record was usable; no substantive full text was retrieved. Claims beyond the abstract are therefore not assessed. [5]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: The abstract reports dialogue-partner commitment updates, but does not expose the full state representation. [5]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: The abstract says commitment-update rules constrain possible dialogue moves; full rules require an accessible paper copy before coding. [5]
Operational Consequence: The abstract situates communication within cooperative activity and multimodal interaction, but does not support a detailed claim about workflow or artifact transitions. [5]
Repair Contestability: Not assessable from the retrieved abstract-level record. [5]
Initial Audit Verdict: Potentially important bridge between commitment dynamics and situated action, but no novelty inference should rely on it until a substantive copy is obtained. [5]

Source: She, Liang & Kang (2026), Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis [6]
Retrieval Status: Substantive preprint text was retrieved and initially extracted; the prior source record also establishes the high-level action-gating mechanism. [6]
Shared Or Actor Indexed State: The system reasons over the user query, tool documentation, prior tool-call history/outcomes, and a proposed tool call; this is provenance context rather than a participant-indexed common-ground state. [6]
Update Or Promotion Mechanism: Misalignment is defined as lack of traceable contextual support for a proposed tool call; the multi-stage pipeline permits execution only when the call is judged aligned. [6]
Operational Consequence: The direct consequence is allow/block control of tool execution before the action occurs. The paper evaluates this guard across two benchmarks and ten backbone LLMs. [6]
Repair Contestability: The retrieved source establishes evidence-gated action control but does not, on the available evidence, establish a multi-party contestation or role-governed shared-state mechanism. [6]
Initial Audit Verdict: Closest predecessor for traceable-evidence action gating. It does not by itself establish common-ground promotion across multiple actors, so its overlap is strongest on PCC’s enforcement and provenance components. [6]
